body:
QUESTION FOR THE LEAD AND THE ADVISOR, P2-29 (1 of 2): THE CONDITION OF Q1 RESTS ON A PREMISE THE CODE CONTRADICTS. Nothing is built; I stopped as told. All of this was READ in the source (background_downloader 9.6.4 Kotlin + this repo), nothing was run.

FACTS
1. No downloader work runs in the foreground. `Config.runInForeground` / `FileDownloader().configure` appear nowhere in app/lib, main.dart, bootstrap.dart or app/android (only `configureNotificationForGroup`, background_downloader_transport.dart:25). So the plugin's size setting stays -1 and `canRunInForeground` is false (TaskRunner.kt:510, which also needs `running != null`); `setForeground` is never called (TaskWorker.kt:140 sets runInForeground=false). The downloader's UIDT path needs task priority 0 (DownloadTask default is 5, our transport sets none), Android 14+ and the RUN_USER_INITIATED_JOBS permission (BDPlugin.kt:173), which the manifest does not declare. The copies are ordinary WorkManager workers and the group card is an ordinary notification: no OS rule needs it. "Long-running WorkManager work needs its own foreground notification" is not how this app is configured. With no `running` state a worker can never be pushed into a foreground start (the condition above).
2. Only a handful of files survive a killed app. `DownloadManager(` is built once (download_providers.dart:256, inside the Dart process), and the only `@pragma('vm:entry-point')` is background_sync.dart:30, which syncs and runs alerts but never the manager. The manager hands the OS at most `maxInFlight = 4` files (download_manager.dart:41, `_pump`). So with the app killed the OS finishes those <= 4 files and nothing starts the rest until the app is opened again. "The phone copy with the app killed" is a tail of <= 4 songs: the same class as the ruled "a single song gets no card". (The transport's doc comment "survive process death" overclaims: audit row, not for this PR.)
3. Why not keep the downloader's card as the closed-app card. Its words are bound to each task at enqueue (static text and {numFinished}-style counters), and native code does not know whether Dart lives, so while the app is open you would get two cards. Giving ours the same id (`"groupNotification"+name`.hashCode(), Notifications.kt:94) makes them overwrite each other: the native one re-posts at every file that ends (Notifications.kt:621), so the card would flip between two texts. And with `running == null` native CANCELS that id (Notifications.kt:629). So "one card" and "the downloader's card survives the kill" cannot both hold.

OPTIONS
A. Accept the tail: group card with no running state, no card for the <= 4 files after a kill. Cost: a silent tail of seconds; with nothing else, a kill leaves no card at all while the server keeps saving.
B. A plus a truthful DATED card posted as soon as the app leaves the foreground (lifecycle), its numbers and its time updating while the process lives, frozen but honest when it is killed ("150 of 214 were ready at 9:03"). A kill then always leaves a card; the phone tail stays silent; the periodic job (6 h) refreshes it. Pure Dart, testable with fakes, stays correct if a foreground service is added later (the ruling already calls the dated card not a stop-gap). Cost: after Home the card stops being live.
C. Keep the downloader's running card: two cards or flicker (3).
D. A foreground service (dataSync, 6 h cap on Android 15) or a UIDT job: manifest, permission, battery, Play review; and the manager dies with the app, so there is little for it to show. Only worth it together with a headless manager (a new item).

RECOMMENDATION: B. Question: accept B (and say so in the amendment of PB-38 and ADR-R44: the group card has no running state, the <= 4 file tail is silent, the dated card is the closed-app card)? Or A, C or D?
